goal: What two things will your classifier tell apart? Pick two objects you can photograph at your desk right now, and avoid things that only differ by color.

steps.label: Try the sandbox first
steps.why: See the idea before you touch the tool: a classifier is just a line that separates two groups.
do: Open the Sandbox tab above.
Drag the line until it separates blue dots from orange dots. Watch Training accuracy climb.
Click 'Skewed sample'. Notice how many different lines separate it perfectly.
Click 'New data (test)'. Watch what happens to a line that looked perfect on skewed data.
Click 'Record my result'.
steps.see: Training accuracy above 90% on the fair sample, and a visible drop when a skewed fit meets new data.

checkpoint.prompt: A line fit on the skewed sample scored 100% in training and much lower on new data. What's the lesson?
options: A model can look perfect on data that never showed it the hard cases
checkpoint.why: The skewed sample hid the hard cases near the boundary, so any line looked perfect. Real data exposed the gap. That's overfitting to a bad sample.

steps.label: Label 20 outfits with a partner
steps.why: Labels feel objective until two people label the same photos. This is where you find out they're decisions.
do: Pair up. Your instructor will put the 20-outfit deck on the screen, one photo at a time.
Without talking, each of you writes F (formal) or C (casual) for every number, 1 to 20.
Compare lists. Count how many numbers you disagreed on.
Pick one you disagreed on and each say, in one sentence, why you chose your label.
steps.see: Two lists of 20 letters and a disagreement count. Most pairs disagree on 3 to 7.

checkpoint.prompt: How many of the 20 did you disagree on? Give one example and say who you think should decide the right label when two sensible people disagree.
checkpoint.placeholder: We disagreed on 5. Number 12 (blazer with jeans): I said formal because of the blazer, my partner said casual because of the jeans. The person who will use the model should decide, and write the rule down.

steps.label: Open Teachable Machine
steps.why: This is a real training tool, used the way you'll see in the lab.
do: Go to teachablemachine.withgoogle.com and click Get Started.
Choose Image Project, then Standard image model.
Rename Class 1 and Class 2 to your two objects (for example 'Mug' and 'Phone').
steps.see: Two class boxes with your names on them, each with a Webcam button, and a Train Model button in the middle.
steps.tip: If the webcam button is grey, your browser blocked the camera. Click the lock icon in the address bar and allow Camera.

checkpoint.prompt: I see two named class boxes and a Train Model button.

steps.label: Collect varied photos
steps.why: Variety in the training data is what makes a model work on new data.
do: Click Webcam under your first class. Hold the object up and press and hold 'Hold to Record' while slowly turning it. Aim for 20 to 30 samples.
Move to a different spot in the room, change the angle, change the background, and record more.
Repeat for the second class.
steps.see: A strip of thumbnails under each class, and the thumbnails don't all look alike.

checkpoint.prompt: Why move around the room while recording?
options: The camera needs to warm up
So the model learns the object, not the background or lighting
checkpoint.why: If every photo of one class has the same background, the model can learn the background as the shortcut. Variety forces it to learn the object.

steps.label: Train and test
do: Click Train Model. Wait for it to finish (under a minute).
In the Preview panel, hold up each object. Watch the confidence bars.
Now hold up something that isn't either object. Watch what it does.
steps.see: Confidence bars that swing toward the right class for your objects. For the unknown object, it still picks one; it has no 'neither' option.

checkpoint.prompt: What did the model say when you showed it an object that was neither class?
checkpoint.placeholder: Example: It said 85% Mug for my water bottle.

steps.label: Break it on purpose with skewed data
steps.why: A model learns the easiest pattern that separates the classes. Tonight you'll hand it a shortcut and watch it take it.
do: Click the three dots on each class and choose Delete all samples.
Re-record your first object with every photo on a dark background (a dark jacket, a dark desk, a bag) and your second object with every photo on a light background (white paper, a bright wall).
Click Train Model again.
Now hold your second object over the dark background. Watch which class wins.
steps.see: The confidence bar swings to the first object even though you're holding the second one. The model learned dark background means object A.
steps.tip: If it still gets it right, your two backgrounds weren't different enough, or you moved the object around too much. Make the trap stronger: same spot, same lighting, one background per class.

checkpoint.prompt: Write one sentence explaining the failure. Name the shortcut the model actually learned instead of your object.
checkpoint.placeholder: The model learned that a dark background means mug, because every mug photo had one, so it never needed to look at the mug.

steps.label: Add a third class and five edge cases
do: Click Add a class. Name it after a third object and record 30 or more varied photos: different angles, distances, and backgrounds.
Click Train Model.
Test five edge cases: both objects in frame, an object half out of frame, an object upside down, a similar object it never saw, and an empty background.
Note which ones it got wrong and what the confidence bars did.
steps.see: At least one edge case gets the wrong answer. On the empty background it still picks a class; it has no 'none of these' option.

checkpoint.placeholder: Example: Far away and the drawing both got labeled as the phone.

steps.label: Fill in your data sheet
steps.why: Real teams document what a model saw and didn't see. You're doing the same.
do: Answer four things: What data did your model see? What did it never see? Three inputs that would fool it. What data would fix each?
Keep it to a few lines each.

checkpoint.prompt: Your data sheet, four parts: (1) what data the model saw, (2) what it never saw, (3) three inputs that would fool it, (4) what training data would fix each of the three.
checkpoint.placeholder: Saw: a blue mug and a black pen, on my desk, from about 40 photos each, mostly from the front in lamp light. Never saw: other mugs, daylight, the pen with its cap off... Fools: a white mug (fix: add mugs of other colors)...

steps.label: Upload a screenshot
do: Take a screenshot of Teachable Machine showing your three classes and the Preview panel with a prediction.
Upload it below.
steps.see: A thumbnail in the submissions list.

stretch: Collect a balanced retraining set (both objects on both backgrounds), retrain, and prove with the same five edge cases that the failures went away.

Sort these four into real-time, serverless, asynchronous, or batch inference and defend each pick: a fraud check as the card is swiped; an internal tool a few staff use a few times an hour; analyzing a 500-page contract someone uploads; re-scoring every customer every Sunday night.
doneWhen: A trained model with three classes
A written failure sentence naming the shortcut the model learned
A screenshot of the Preview panel with a prediction uploaded

submission.prompt: Upload a screenshot of your trained model's preview.

lens.plain: Learning with an answer key, learning without one by finding groups, and learning from rewards.
lens.exam: Domain 1, Objective 1.1.5: describe different types of AI/ML learning. Objective 1.2.3 pairs them with regression, classification, and clustering.

lens.plain: Training is the model studying the examples. Inferencing is the trained model answering on new input, every time anyone uses it.
lens.exam: Domain 1, Objective 1.1.1: training and inferencing are listed as basic terms to define.
Domain 1, Objective 1.1.3: describe various types of inferencing. Expect a scenario and 'which one fits'.

lens.term: Data types: labeled and unlabeled, structured and unstructured, tabular, time series, image, text
lens.plain: Does each example come with the answer? Is it rows and columns or free-form? A spreadsheet, a measurement over time, a photo, or words.
lens.exam: Domain 1, Objective 1.1.4: describe the different types of data in AI models.

lens.plain: Overfit memorized the practice test and fails the real one. Underfit never studied and fails both. High variance vs high bias.
lens.exam: Domain 4, Objective 4.1.6: describe effects of bias and variance, including overfitting and underfitting. Also shows up in Domain 1 model-evaluation questions.

quiz.q: Your classifier learned that 'mug' means 'brown background' because every mug photo had one. This is an example of:
a: A shortcut learned from skewed training data
quiz.why: The model found the easiest pattern that separated the classes. That pattern was the background, not the object.

quiz.q: Which type of learning uses examples that already have the correct answer attached?
quiz.why: Supervised learning trains on labeled examples. Unsupervised finds groups without labels. Reinforcement learns from rewards. 'Generative' isn't a type of learning at all; it's a thing a trained model can do.

quiz.q: A model scores 99% on its training photos and 60% on new photos. What's the most likely problem?
a: The model needs a bigger GPU
quiz.why: A big gap between training and new data is the signature of overfitting.

quiz.q: Two people label the same photos and disagree on 4 of 20. What does this tell you?
a: Labels are human decisions, and the model learns whatever decisions it's given
quiz.why: Labels encode judgment. If the labelers disagree, the model inherits that fuzziness.

quiz.q: A bank wants a fraud score the instant a card is swiped. Which inference option fits?
quiz.why: Real-time inference returns an answer in milliseconds and stays on. Serverless also answers fast but can have a cold-start delay after idle time, which a card swipe can't afford. Asynchronous queues the request. Batch runs on a schedule.

tools.name: Teachable Machine
tools.use: Train a two- or three-class image classifier from your webcam in the browser, no code.
tools.free: Free, no account needed. Training runs in your browser so photos stay on your laptop. Optional Google sign-in only if you want to save the project to Drive. Checked October 7, 2026.

cards.a: Learning from examples that come with the right answer attached. The model guesses, checks the label, adjusts, and repeats. Spam filters, fraud flags, and photo tagging are supervised.

Learning from data with no labels. The model looks for natural groups on its own, like sorting a million shoppers into segments nobody named in advance. The exam word for the main technique is clustering.
Learning from rewards and penalties instead of an answer key. The system tries an action, sees the result, and does more of what paid off. Game-playing AI and robots learning to walk use it.

cards.q: Is generative AI a fourth type of machine learning?
cards.a: No. Supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement are ways a machine learns. Generative AI is something a model can do once trained, and chat assistants were trained using all three. If a question lists it beside the learning types, it's the distractor.

cards.q: Which technique fits a problem with no labels where you want to discover groups?
cards.a: Clustering. Classification needs known categories to assign; regression predicts a number. Clustering is for when the categories don't exist yet and you want the data to suggest them.

cards.q: What's the difference between training and inferencing?
cards.a: Training is the model studying examples and adjusting itself: slow, costly, done once or occasionally. Inferencing is the trained model answering on new input: fast, cheap, every time anyone uses it. Asking a chat assistant a question is inference.

cards.q: When would you choose real-time inference?
cards.a: When you need an answer in milliseconds and the endpoint must always be on, like a fraud check as a card is swiped or a product recommendation as a page loads.

cards.q: When would you choose serverless inference?
cards.a: When traffic is bursty with idle gaps and a short cold-start delay is acceptable. It scales to zero when nobody's using it, so you don't pay for an always-on server. An internal tool used a few times an hour.

cards.q: When would you choose asynchronous inference?
cards.a: When requests are large or slow (up to about 1 GB and up to an hour of processing) and near-real-time is fine. You drop off the request and pick up the result, like analyzing a 500-page PDF.

cards.q: When would you choose batch inference?
cards.a: When you want predictions for a whole dataset at once and don't need a live endpoint, like re-scoring every customer in the database every Sunday night. In SageMaker AI this is a batch transform job.

cards.q: What's the difference between structured and unstructured data?
cards.a: Structured data fits rows and columns, like a spreadsheet or database table. Unstructured data is free-form: text, images, audio, video. Most of the world's data is unstructured, and deep learning is what made it usable.

cards.q: What does 'labeled data' mean, and why does it matter?
cards.a: Each example comes with the correct answer already marked by a person. Labeled data makes supervised learning possible. Labels are human decisions, so a model inherits every inconsistency in how people labeled.
Measurements taken in order over time, like daily sales, hourly temperature, or a heartbeat trace. The order matters, which is why forecasting models treat it differently from a plain table.

cards.q: What is overfitting, and what does it look like in the numbers?
cards.a: The model memorized the specifics of its training data instead of learning the general pattern. The tell is a big gap: very high accuracy on training data, much lower on new data. In exam language, high variance. The usual fix is more varied data.

The model is too simple or saw too little data to find the pattern at all, so it does badly on training data and new data alike. In exam language, high bias. Fixes include a more capable model, better features, or more training.

cards.q: Why do you hold back a test set?
cards.a: To measure how the model does on data it has never seen. Testing on training data only tells you how well it memorized. The gap between training and test performance is how you catch overfitting.

practice.q: A retailer has a year of purchase records but no customer categories. Marketing wants to discover natural customer groups to target. Which type of machine learning is this?
practice.why: No labels and a goal of finding groups the data suggests: unsupervised learning, specifically clustering.
wrong: Supervised needs labeled examples. There are no categories to learn from.
Reinforcement learns from rewards for actions. Nothing here is acting.
Generative AI is not a type of learning. It's a distractor on this kind of question.

practice.q: A company trains a model on 50,000 past insurance claims, each already marked 'legitimate' or 'fraudulent,' so it can flag new claims. Which learning type and technique is this?
practice.why: Each example has a label (legitimate or fraudulent), and the output is one of two categories: supervised classification.
wrong: There are labels, so it's not unsupervised, and the categories are already known.
Reinforcement learning uses rewards from actions, not a labeled dataset.
Regression predicts a number. This predicts a category.

practice.q: A payment processor must decide whether to approve a card transaction within 200 milliseconds while the customer waits at the register. Which SageMaker AI inference option is MOST appropriate?
practice.why: A hard latency requirement with the user waiting calls for an always-on real-time endpoint.
wrong: Batch runs on a whole dataset on a schedule. The customer would be long gone.
Asynchronous queues the request and returns later. Too slow for a register.
Serverless can cold-start after idle periods, adding seconds of delay. A card swipe can't absorb that.

practice.q: A law firm's tool lets staff upload contracts of several hundred pages for AI analysis. Each request can take several minutes to process, and a result within 10 minutes is acceptable. Which inference option fits BEST?
practice.why: Large payloads and long processing with near-real-time (not instant) expectations is exactly what asynchronous inference is designed for.
wrong: Real-time endpoints time out on multi-minute requests and have payload limits.
Serverless also has payload and duration limits that a several-hundred-page document would exceed.
Batch is for a whole dataset on a schedule, not an individual upload that someone is waiting on.

practice.q: A company needs to recalculate a churn-risk score for all 3 million customers once a week. No one needs individual results on demand. Which option is MOST cost-effective?
practice.why: Whole dataset, on a schedule, no live endpoint needed: batch transform, which spins up only for the job.
wrong: An always-on endpoint would sit idle all week and cost money for nothing.
Asynchronous handles individual large requests, not a scheduled sweep of millions of rows.
Serverless is for bursty on-demand traffic, not a planned bulk job.

practice.q: A hospital wants to predict patient no-shows using appointment records stored in a database with columns for date, department, age, and prior no-shows. What type of data is this?
practice.why: Rows and columns in a database is structured, tabular data.
wrong: There are no images involved.
The data is in fixed columns, not free-form text.
The records include past no-show outcomes, so they can serve as labels, and a table of appointments isn't a time series of one measurement.

practice.q: A model achieves 99% accuracy on its training data and 62% on a held-out test set. Which statement BEST describes the problem and the likely fix?
a: Overfitting; add more varied training data or simplify the model
Data leakage; delete the test set
The test set is wrong; evaluate on training data instead
practice.why: A large gap between training and test accuracy is the signature of overfitting (high variance). More diverse data or a simpler model are standard remedies.
wrong: Underfitting shows poor performance on both sets, not a big gap.
Deleting the test set removes your only honest measurement.
Evaluating on training data hides the problem instead of fixing it.

practice.q: A model performs poorly on both its training data and new data. Which term describes this, and what is a reasonable next step?
a: Underfitting; use a more capable model or better features
High variance; reduce the training data
practice.why: Bad on both sets means the model never captured the pattern: underfitting, or high bias. A more expressive model, better features, or more training helps.
wrong: Overfitting is good on training and bad on new data, not bad on both.
High variance is the overfitting side. Reducing data would make things worse.
Nondeterminism is a generative AI limitation, unrelated to fit.

practice.q: A company uses a trained demand-forecasting model every morning to generate the day's inventory orders. Which term describes what happens each morning?
practice.why: Using a trained model on new input to get predictions is inference. Training already happened.
wrong: Training adjusts the model from examples. Nothing is being re-learned each morning.
Labeling means attaching correct answers to examples, a data-preparation step.
Feature engineering is choosing or shaping the inputs before training.

practice.q: Which pair correctly matches a data type to an example?
a: Time-series data: a customer's mailing address
Unstructured data: a spreadsheet of monthly sales
Labeled data: product photos each tagged with the product's category
Tabular data: a folder of recorded phone calls
practice.why: Photos with a category attached to each are labeled data, ready for supervised learning.
wrong: An address is a plain field, not a measurement over time.
A spreadsheet is structured, tabular data.
Recorded calls are unstructured audio, not a table.

items.label: Three-class model trained on varied photos
good: Your model has three working classes and the photos are varied, {name}. That's the clean baseline the rest of the lab needs.
Nice variety in your training photos, {name}. Different angles and backgrounds are what keep a model honest.
fix: Your training photos look like they came from one spot. Move around, change the background, and retrain before you break it.
Add more variety to each class: angles, distances, backgrounds. Thirty varied photos beats a hundred identical ones.

items.label: Failure sentence names the shortcut the model learned
good: "{quote}" names the exact shortcut, {name}. That sentence is the whole lab.
fix: Your failure sentence says it got confused, but not what it learned instead. Name the shortcut: the background, the lighting, the angle.
Say what the model actually latched onto. 'It learned dark background means mug' is the kind of sentence I'm after.

items.label: Four-part data sheet; every fix is training data
good: Your data sheet is specific about what the model never saw, {name}, and every fix is new training data. That's the right instinct.
The fixes on your data sheet are all data, not settings, {name}. That's exactly the point.
fix: Your fixes describe changing settings or training longer. A data problem needs data: which photos would you add for each one?
Each fix should be training data you'd collect. 'Retrain it' isn't a fix; 'add 20 photos of the mug on a dark background' is.

items.label: Five edge cases tested; screenshot submitted
good: Good edge-case testing, {name}. "{quote}" tells me you actually pushed on it.
You tested the weird cases, {name}, which is where models break.
fix: List which of the five edge cases fooled it and what the confidence bars did. That's your evidence.
Try all five edge cases and note which ones it got wrong. Even 'it got all five right' is worth writing down.

rubric.allMet: This is complete, {name}. For the Stretch, retrain on a balanced set and prove the same edge cases now pass.
